article_title: Helping English Learners Rise to the Challenge of Complex Texts
citation: Helping English Learners Rise to the Challenge of Complex Texts. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 14, No. 3. http://ell.stanford.edu/teaching_resources/ela
title: Apprenticeship model with tailored scaffolding builds ELL students' autonomy with complex texts
description: The unit emphasizes the apprenticeship model of learning, in which students participate in guided academic practices deliberately designed to provide opportunities for students to become autonomous experts over time. Teachers offer various levels of support, or scaffolding, tailored to each student's needs, and students progressively develop their ability to work independently. Students move from informal and collaborative group settings to formal group and individual presentations, practicing articulating ideas, interpreting information, and presenting and defending claims.
requirements: Scaffolding must be tailored to each student's needs
target_learners: secondary English language learners
target_learning_goals: independent academic reading and writing
articulating ideas and defending claims
examples: Assessments such as peer editing with clearly defined rubrics or finding textual evidence to support conclusions are designed to build students' autonomy as purposeful readers and writers over time.
key_sources: Helping English Learners Rise to the Challenge of Complex Texts. (2014). WestEd R&D Alert, Vol. 14, No. 3. http://ell.stanford.edu/teaching_resources/ela

article_title: Growing Strong Learners in Galt Joint Union Elementary School District
citation: McCarthy, E., Morgan, C. & Sussman, J. (2020). Growing strong learners in Galt Joint Union Elementary School District. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://www.wested.org
title: Academic Parent-Teacher Teams (APTT) dual-capacity building program
description: APTT is a family-engagement model in which teachers lead group parent meetings, share child assessment data against kindergarten-readiness benchmarks, and teach parents games to build targeted skills at home. The article describes that "teachers lead three group parent meetings throughout the year where parents learn about their child's curriculum, become better acquainted with each other and the teacher, and plan for supporting learning at home." Parents leave with their own game pieces and see progress data at the next meeting.
requirements: Teachers receive specialized training in implementing APTT meetings and activities, with trainer support across the school year
constraints: Implementation of the third APTT meeting was not possible due to COVID-19 shelter-in-place guidelines
target_learners: Pre-K children aged 3 to 5, including English learners, at Fairsite Preschool
target_learning_goals: Kindergarten readiness in language and literacy, mathematics, social-emotional, self-regulation, and physical development
examples: Teachers shared assessment data, parents played learning games, and families took home game pieces; parents who missed meetings reviewed content individually with a teacher or administrator
key_sources: McCarthy, E., Morgan, C. & Sussman, J. (2020). Growing strong learners in Galt Joint Union Elementary School District. San Francisco, CA: WestEd. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=ED613373

article_title: A Framework for Institutional Change in the Age of AI
citation: Perl-Nussbaum, D., & Finkelstein, N. D. (2026). A framework for institutional change in the age of AI. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00649-4
title: Organize AI-era reform around pedagogical approaches rather than specific tools
description: Because AI capabilities change on timescales of months and findings about specific tools risk obsolescence before publication, change should focus on pedagogical orientations and practices that survive replacement of any particular model or platform. The article states: "AI driven change should focus on approaches rather than tools – pedagogical orientations and practices that can survive the replacement of any particular model or platform". Institutions should invest in sustained faculty inquiry support rather than tool procurement.
requirements: Drawing on the stable IE evidence base (student engagement, authentic practice, epistemology) that does not become obsolete with new model releases
constraints: Course policies around AI use should be developed through ongoing dialogue and revisited as tools evolve, while still maintaining coherent ethics and integrity principles
target_learners: STEM faculty, departmental leaders, institutional decision-makers
target_learning_goals: Durable pedagogical practice amid rapidly changing AI tools
examples: In the workshop case study, sessions were organized around policy, norm-setting, and homework-correction guidance rather than specific platforms, treating tool-comparison questions as secondary
key_sources: Perl-Nussbaum, D., & Finkelstein, N. D. (2026). A framework for institutional change in the age of AI. International Journal of STEM Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s40594-026-00649-4

article_title: Beyond prior knowledge: the predictive role of knowledge-building in tutor learning
citation: Fathima Ameen, Tasmia Shahriar, Aditi Mallavarapu, Shiyan Jiang, Noboru Matsuda. (2026). Beyond prior knowledge: the predictive role of knowledge-building in tutor learning. Behaviormetrika. https://doi.org/10.1007/s41237-026-00294-9
title: APLUS: a learning-by-teaching environment in which students tutor SimStudent to solve algebraic equations
description: APLUS (Artificial Peer Learning Using SimStudent) is an online learning-by-teaching environment in which students, acting as tutors, "teach a virtual agent named SimStudent to solve algebraic equations through guided problem solving". SimStudent learns production rules via programming by demonstration (inductive logic programming), proposes solution steps, and asks focal questions when the tutor disagrees or lacks a production. Tutors can quiz SimStudent across four quiz levels and access a Problem Bank, Unit Overview, Introduction Video, worked Examples, and a meta-tutor agent, Mr. Williams, who gives voluntary metacognitive hints.
requirements: SimStudent is pre-trained on a small set of one-step equations to establish baseline knowledge before tutoring begins
constraints: In the version used in the study, solution steps allow only four basic math operations: add, subtract, multiply, and divide by a term
target_learners: middle school students (grades 6–8)
target_learning_goals: algebraic equation solving
effective tutoring and self-regulated learning strategies
examples: Mr. Williams might hint, "SimStudent failed on the two-step equation. Teaching similar equations will help him pass that quiz item."
key_sources: Fathima Ameen, Tasmia Shahriar, Aditi Mallavarapu, Shiyan Jiang, Noboru Matsuda. (2026). Beyond prior knowledge: the predictive role of knowledge-building in tutor learning. Behaviormetrika. https://doi.org/10.1007/s41237-026-00294-9

article_title: Rethinking AI-assisted writing instruction: feedback literacy scripts, calibration training, and student writing development
citation: Dai (2026). Rethinking AI-assisted writing instruction: feedback literacy scripts, calibration training, and student writing development. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1829268
title: APCA Assessment-Performance Calibration Activity
description: APCA is a self-assessment calibration training organized around "a process of “self-assessment-comparison-adjustment,” requiring students to repeatedly compare their own judgments with external evaluations across multiple task rounds". It has four stages: Anchor (reviewing sample texts at different quality levels), Predict (estimating one's score and confidence), Compare (identifying judgment bias against teacher ratings), and Adjust (modifying evaluation strategies based on recurring over- or underestimation). Each round lasted approximately 10 to 15 minutes with structured calibration logs, implemented continuously from T0 to T3, with log completion exceeding 90% per round.
requirements: Students complete structured calibration logs recording predicted score, confidence judgment, discrepancy from the teacher rating, and reflection on recurring bias, reviewed against a unified feedback protocol
constraints: The APCA group showed lower raw self-assessment error at baseline, so analyses used baseline-adjusted models; self-assessment and comparison stages were retained at T3 even though AI support was withdrawn
target_learners: undergraduate English majors with basic academic writing skills
target_learning_goals: accurate self-assessment of writing quality
reduction of overconfidence in self-judgment
examples: In each round students completed a calibration log and the researcher provided brief written comments for use in the next task
key_sources: Dai (2026). Rethinking AI-assisted writing instruction: feedback literacy scripts, calibration training, and student writing development. Frontiers in Psychology. https://doi.org/10.3389/fpsyg.2026.1829268

article_title: Fostering Self-Directed Growth with Generative AI: Toward a New Learning Analytics Framework
citation: Qianrun Mao. (2024). Fostering Self-Directed Growth with Generative AI: Toward a New Learning Analytics Framework. https://www.google.com/search?q=Fostering+Self-Directed+Growth+with+Generative+AI+Toward+a+New+Learning+Analytics+Framework
title: Aspire to Potential Scoring Rubric (APSR): a GAI-applied diagnostic rubric with undisclosed scores
description: Within the diagnostic analytics layer, the GAI evaluates students' summative self-assessment frameworks using the pre-designed Aspire to Potential Scoring Rubric (APSR), which "incorporates component weights, relational logistics, and vectorized progression, all mapped both within and across the phases of the SDL cycles". Component relevance, relational logistics, and vectorized progression refer to tailored assessment of each element's relative importance, their interconnections, and progression through key A2PL stages. Importantly, the GAI's scoring assessment is not disclosed to learners; interactive analytics build on the scores to deliver feedback.
requirements: Scores must remain undisclosed to learners so that feedback promotes guided discovery rather than direct evaluation
constraints: The article notes this is a proposed design; empirical validation and platform engineering are reserved for future research
target_learners: learners driving their own SDL cycles with GAI support
target_learning_goals: progression of summative self-assessment frameworks aligned with personal goals
key_sources: Qianrun Mao. (2024). Fostering Self-Directed Growth with Generative AI: Toward a New Learning Analytics Framework. https://www.google.com/search?q=Fostering+Self-Directed+Growth+with+Generative+AI+Toward+a+New+Learning+Analytics+Framework

article_title: Human-written and AI-generated revisions: An appraisal analysis of dialogic positioning in argumentative writing
citation: Zhao H and Ji J (2026) Human-written and AI-generated revisions: an appraisal analysis of dialogic positioning in argumentative writing. Front. Educ. 11:1904852. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1904852
title: Appraisal Theory (Martin and White, 2005) as a framework for analyzing evaluative meaning and dialogic positioning
description: Appraisal Theory extends the interpersonal metafunction within Systemic Functional Linguistics and, as the article states, "provides a comprehensive framework for analyzing evaluative meaning in discourse". It comprises three subsystems — Attitude (Affect, Judgement, Appreciation), Engagement (Monoglossic vs. Heteroglossic, with Contract and Expand), and Graduation (Force and Focus). The study applies it, with particular focus on Engagement, to code 16,234 appraisal instances across 168 essays and compare dialogic positioning across draft types.
requirements: Manual coding of sentences against the appraisal categories, with coding decisions informed by surrounding context rather than surface forms alone
constraints: Justify is a later extension to the Proclaim system introduced by White (2012), not part of the original framework
target_learners: undergraduate EFL English majors
target_learning_goals: constructing authorial stance and dialogic positioning in argumentative writing
examples: Coders classified believe as Pronounce in one sentence and as Attribute-Acknowledge in another, depending on context
key_sources: Zhao H and Ji J (2026) Human-written and AI-generated revisions: an appraisal analysis of dialogic positioning in argumentative writing. Front. Educ. 11:1904852. https://doi.org/10.3389/feduc.2026.1904852

article_title: Evidence and Theory for why the Best Example-Problem Ratio To Optimize Learning Gain Depends on Knowledge Content
citation: Rachatasumrit, N., Koedinger, K. R., & Carvalho, P. F. (2023). Evidence and theory for why the best example-problem ratio to optimize learning gain depends on knowledge content. https://osf.io/29wpe
title: Apprentice Learner (AL) computational framework with an added memory mechanism as an executable theory of example-versus-practice learning
description: The AL framework is a computational architecture in which simulated learners acquire and refine if-then production rules through induction: when no rule fits a problem state, the agent requests a demonstration and translates the example into a new rule, and performance feedback prompts refinement of rule conditions. This work added a memory mechanism based on Pavlik and Anderson's ACT-R memory model, giving rules an activation strength with trial ages and decay rates so that recall is stochastic and rules can be forgotten. The article uses AL agents trained on the same four conditions as human participants as an executable theory that reproduces the cross-over interaction.
requirements: Some minimal feedback is required: without any signal the model cannot update memory traces or refine over-general rules
constraints: The simulation simplified problem encoding to parsed input states (e.g., shape type, line lengths), assuming diagram parsing is prior knowledge humans bring
target_learners: Simulated K-12 learners of math and geometry content
target_learning_goals: Fact memorization
Skill acquisition via induction from worked examples
examples: Agents pretrained to match human pretest performance (M = 0.59 and 0.60 for facts and skills) completed 16 pretest questions, 4 study sessions, and 16 posttest questions after a waiting period
key_sources: Rachatasumrit, N., Koedinger, K. R., & Carvalho, P. F. (2023). Evidence and theory for why the best example-problem ratio to optimize learning gain depends on knowledge content. https://osf.io/29wpe

article_title: Game-Based and Gamified Robotics Education: A Comparative Systematic Review and Design Guidelines
citation: Syed Tanzim Mubarrat, Byung-Cheol Min, Tianyu Shao, E. Cho Smith, Bedrich Benes, Alejandra J. Magana, Christos Mousas, and Dominic Kao. (2026). Game-Based and Gamified Robotics Education: A Comparative Systematic Review and Design Guidelines. Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3791338
title: Approach–context–pedagogy coupling framework for game-based and gamified robotics education
description: The review's organizing framework holds that instructional approach (GBL vs. gamification), learning context (formal vs. informal), and pedagogical model are coupled in robotics education: "GBL more prevalent in informal settings, while gamification dominated formal classrooms" and gamification "favored project-based learning". The framework maps three dominant pedagogies — experiential learning, project-based learning, and constructivist learning — onto approaches and contexts, with formal classrooms leaning toward PBL-driven designs and informal settings favoring experiential approaches with higher proportions of constructivist elements.
requirements: Coding of studies requires classifying approach (using Deterding et al. and Sailer and Homner definitions), learning context (based on the intervention rather than the evaluation design), and pedagogical model for each study.
constraints: The association is descriptive of the 2014–2025 corpus of 95 studies; the review reports it as an observed pattern with χ² tests, not as a causal account.
target_learners: K-12 through graduate learners in formal and informal robotics settings
target_learning_goals: robotics-related skills including programming, software development, and understanding of robotic systems
examples: The review's 2×2 contingency analyses showed approach × context was significant (χ²(1)=14.16, p<0.001, Cramer's V = 0.37) and PBL was more frequent in gamified studies (χ²(1)=6.76, p=.009).
key_sources: Syed Tanzim Mubarrat, Byung-Cheol Min, Tianyu Shao, E. Cho Smith, Bedrich Benes, Alejandra J. Magana, Christos Mousas, and Dominic Kao. (2026). Game-Based and Gamified Robotics Education: A Comparative Systematic Review and Design Guidelines. Proceedings of the 2026 CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems (CHI '26). https://doi.org/10.1145/3772318.3791338

article_title: Teaching and Learning in the Social Context: A Meta-Analysis of Service Learning's Effects on Academic, Personal, Social, and Citizenship Outcomes
citation: Ruíz Montero, P. J., & Bru Serrano, M. (2021). La educación física y el deporte como servicio hacia los más vulnerables: beneficios del aprendizaje-servicio. Red Euroamericana de Investigación y Docencia en Educación Física. https://www.riadis.es
title: La metodología Aprendizaje-Servicio (ApS) como marco para desarrollar competencias prácticas y valores en estudiantes universitarios
description: El catálogo presenta el Aprendizaje-Servicio (ApS) como metodología socioeducativa aplicada desde la educación física y el deporte. Según el prólogo, "Dicha metodología permite, desde la práctica socioeducativa, y en este caso vinculada también a la educación física y el deporte, fomentar en los estudiantes competencias prácticas relacionadas con un mayor compromiso con la sociedad así como valores de igualdad, respecto, tolerancia y justicia social". Los proyectos descritos la aplican con estudiantes del Doble Grado en Educación Primaria y Ciencias de la Actividad Física y del Deporte que intervienen con colectivos vulnerables.
requirements: Intervenciones prácticas con colectivos vulnerables en las que el alumnado ofrece un servicio mientras trabaja contenido curricular de diversas asignaturas
constraints: Se documenta en el contexto específico de la Ciudad Autónoma de Melilla y sus centros colaboradores (CETI, Centro Asistencial Gota de Leche)
target_learners: estudiantes universitarios del Doble Grado en Educación Primaria y Ciencias de la Actividad Física y del Deporte
target_learning_goals: compromiso con la sociedad
valores de igualdad, respeto, tolerancia y justicia social
aplicación práctica de contenido curricular
examples: Proyectos FIDO 2022 y de inclusión del colectivo migrante de la UGR en Melilla, coordinados por Pedro Jesús Ruíz Montero
key_sources: Ruíz Montero, P. J., & Bru Serrano, M. (2021). La educación física y el deporte como servicio hacia los más vulnerables: beneficios del aprendizaje-servicio. Red Euroamericana de Investigación y Docencia en Educación Física. https://www.riadis.es

article_title: Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context
citation: Olivia Brown, Nicola Power, and Julie Gore. (2024). Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context. Organizational Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.1177/10944281241271216
title: Applied Cognitive Task Analysis (ACTA): task diagram, knowledge audit, and cognitive demands table
description: ACTA is an interview technique designed to identify the key cognitive elements required to perform expert tasks, typically in three phases: developing a task diagram, a knowledge audit interview, and data analysis with knowledge representation. Task Diagrams contain three to seven steps aligned with short-term memory; the Knowledge Audit probes aspects of expertise such as big picture, noticing, job smarts, improvising, self-monitoring, and anomalies. Findings are represented in a Cognitive Demands Table highlighting common challenges, errors, and solutions, which can inform future training and job design. ACTA is streamlined and suited to instances in which time is limited.
requirements: A minimum of three to five experts are needed to identify expert cognitive processes
The researcher and participant must identify an incident too complex for a novice to complete
constraints: Participants often find the task diagram phase challenging and offer too much detail, requiring the interviewer to keep the conversation on track
target_learners: High-performing experts completing domain-specific tasks
target_learning_goals: Documenting expert cues and strategies for complex workplace tasks
examples: Osland et al. used ACTA with ten global leadership experts plus ten confirmatory experts, obtaining over 30 hours of Knowledge Audit interview data
key_sources: Olivia Brown, Nicola Power, and Julie Gore. (2024). Cognitive Task Analysis: Eliciting Expert Cognition in Context. Organizational Research Methods. https://doi.org/10.1177/10944281241271216

article_title: Designing multimedia learning environments using animated pedagogical agents: factors and issues.
citation: Woo, H.L. (2009). Designing multimedia learning environments using animated pedagogical agents: factors and issues. Journal of Computer Assisted Learning, 25, 203-218. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2729.2008.00299.x
title: The APL framework for organizing APA research
description: The APL framework organizes research on animated pedagogical agents around three areas analogous to classroom elements: 'A represents APA characteristics', 'P represents Presentation by the APA', and 'L represents Learners' characteristics'. It is derived from the four fundamental classroom elements (teacher, teaching, students, physical environment), dropping the invariant physical environment. The paper uses it to structure its review of controversial findings and factors in APA-based learning environments.
requirements: An APA must be situated in a learning system that provides support for its instructional rendering, since unlike a real teacher it cannot exist alone
constraints: The APA physical environment is quite invariant and confined to working with a computer and its peripherals, so it is excluded from the framework
target_learners: online and multimedia learners
target_learning_goals: understanding factors affecting APA-based learning environments
examples: The paper reviews anthropomorphism, appearance, modality, agent multiplicity, speech-gesture cooperation, and sensory preference under the three framework areas
key_sources: Woo, H.L. (2009). Designing multimedia learning environments using animated pedagogical agents: factors and issues. Journal of Computer Assisted Learning, 25, 203-218. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2729.2008.00299.x

article_title: Designing multimedia learning environments using animated pedagogical agents: factors and issues.
citation: Woo, H.L. (2009). Designing multimedia learning environments using animated pedagogical agents: factors and issues. Journal of Computer Assisted Learning, 25, 203-218. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2729.2008.00299.x
title: Design APA instruction by analysing affordances and matching what agents offer to what users need
description: The paper recommends that APA technology be viewed under the lens of affordance, meaning 'opportunity for action', rather than as a holistic human substitute. Design should begin by analysing the affordances of APAs, then establish a proper match between what the APAs can offer and what the users need, taking learners' background characteristics into account. Under this view, agents with less humanlikeness for specific learning types such as storytelling, short demonstration, or enactment of a scene are seen as tools, so learners impose fewer social expectations and are more amenable to learning with them.
requirements: Design must begin with analysing the affordances of APAs, followed by establishing a proper match between what the APAs can offer and what the users need
constraints: Whether users use the technology's features depends on their prior experience, age level, past domain knowledge, culture, and intention; the technology only offers the opportunity but will not necessarily result in an action
target_learners: online learners using agent-based multimedia environments
target_learning_goals: effective design of agent-based instruction matched to learner needs
examples: The paper suggests using agents with less adaptivity or less humanlikeness for very specific types of learning, such as storytelling, short demonstration, or enactment of a scene
key_sources: Woo, H.L. (2009). Designing multimedia learning environments using animated pedagogical agents: factors and issues. Journal of Computer Assisted Learning, 25, 203-218. https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2729.2008.00299.x

article_title: Apprenticeship as a developmental mechanism in argumentation skill development
citation: Song, Yu. (2023). Apprenticeship As a Developmental Mechanism in Argumentation Skill Development. Ph.D. dissertation, Columbia University. https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/Song_columbia_0054D_18218
title: Apprenticeship model of dialogic argumentation skill development
description: The dissertation proposes an apprenticeship model as a mechanism in the development of skill in dialogic argumentation, in which less skilled adolescents engage in one-on-one dialogs with more skilled partners who model "skilled forms of counterargument and use of evidence to support claims" along with questioning and meta-talk. The skill developed dialogically is treated as "a bridge to individual written argument". The model was tested in a multi-week intervention with more skilled versus similarly skilled anonymous partners.
requirements: Learners must engage in extended one-on-one electronic dialogs on controversial issues with partners who display skilled argumentative moves.
constraints: The abstract presents the model as tested with young adolescents on controversial issues; it does not claim generalization beyond this population or format.
target_learners: young adolescents
target_learning_goals: dialogic argumentation skill
individual written argument
examples: Young adolescents were paired with a series of both more skilled and similarly skilled partners, anonymously, in multi-week one-on-one electronic dialogs on controversial issues.
key_sources: Song, Yu. (2023). Apprenticeship As a Developmental Mechanism in Argumentation Skill Development. Ph.D. dissertation, Columbia University. https://academiccommons.columbia.edu/doi/Song_columbia_0054D_18218

article_title: The role of metacognitive experience: Can feedback training affect kindergarteners'monitoring accuracy?
citation: Kristin Kolloff, Ebru Ger, Claudia M. Roebers. (2025). The role of metacognitive experience: Can feedback training affect kindergarteners' monitoring accuracy? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09422-4
title: App-based metacognitive monitoring training program with paired-associates memory tasks and feedback
description: A computerized, self-paced training program delivered on tablet computers in which children completed paired-associates memory learning tasks (learning, delay, recognition, monitoring, and feedback phases) across 12 sessions. The article describes it as "a computerized method that is modern, economical in terms of human resources, and allows upscaling." Feedback was delivered visually (green tick, red cross) and auditorily depending on condition; the active control group completed a Hearts and Flowers executive function task instead.
requirements: Some adult supervision during sessions, per the article's own note
Trained research assistants for technical setup and instructions
constraints: The active control group did not participate in any memory tasks during training sessions
target_learners: kindergarten-aged children (5.5 to 7.7 years)
target_learning_goals: metacognitive monitoring accuracy
confidence judgment calibration
examples: Children learned 12 paired associations per session (eight in session one), studied each picture pair for five seconds, completed a one-minute delay activity, took an untimed recognition test, and rated confidence on a 4-point smiley scale
key_sources: Kristin Kolloff, Ebru Ger, Claudia M. Roebers. (2025). The role of metacognitive experience: Can feedback training affect kindergarteners' monitoring accuracy? Metacognition and Learning. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11409-025-09422-4

article_title: Using student-centred learning environments to stimulate deep approaches to learning: Factors encouraging or discouraging their effectiveness
citation: Baeten, M., Kyndt, E., Struyven, K., & Dochy, F. (2010). Using student-centred learning environments to stimulate deep approaches to learning: Factors encouraging or discouraging their effectiveness. Educational Research Review, 5, 243–260. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2010.06.001
title: Approaches to learning framework: deep and surface approaches combining intention, motive and strategy
description: The review organises its synthesis around the approaches-to-learning construct, in which "An approach to learning embeds the intention of the student when starting a task and the learning processes and strategies used to carry out a task". Deep approaches combine an intention to understand with meaning-seeking strategies; surface approaches combine an intention to reproduce with rote memorisation and minimal effort. Approaches are measured by ASI- and SPQ-based questionnaires and are context-dependent rather than stable traits, which is why the review examines environmental and student factors shaping them.
requirements: Measurement by self-report questionnaires based on the ASI and SPQ traditions
constraints: Approaches depend on the context within which a task is experienced and the learner's interpretation thereof; recent SPQ research supports a two-factor deep/surface structure without a separate strategic scale
target_learners: Higher education students
target_learning_goals: Fostering deep, meaningful learning and understanding rather than reproduction of content
examples: The review used this framework to select studies measuring approaches with ASI- and SPQ-based inventories and to classify encouraging and discouraging factors across context, perception and student characteristics
key_sources: Baeten, M., Kyndt, E., Struyven, K., & Dochy, F. (2010). Using student-centred learning environments to stimulate deep approaches to learning: Factors encouraging or discouraging their effectiveness. Educational Research Review, 5, 243–260. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.edurev.2010.06.001

article_title: The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development
citation: Sarit Barzilai & Clark A. Chinn. (2024). The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09927-5
title: The Apt-AIR framework unpacks fully apt epistemic performance into five interwoven aspects of competent engagement with aims, ideals, and reliable processes
description: The Apt-AIR framework was developed to address the normative question of what the goals of epistemic education should be. It proposes that fully apt epistemic performance is facilitated by five interwoven aspects of competent engagement with aims, ideals, and reliable processes: cognitive engagement, adapting epistemic performance across tasks and contexts, metacognitively regulating and understanding epistemic performance, caring about and enjoying epistemic performance, and participating in epistemic performance with others. The article states that "the aspects are interrelated and are not independent or mutually exclusive dimensions" and that the heuristic value is "to identify important aspects of epistemic performance that require instructional support."
requirements: Instructional designers must consider how each aspect of epistemic performance connects to specific aims, ideals, and reliable processes rather than treating the aspects as free-standing skills
constraints: The order in which the five aspects are presented does not reflect their importance or temporal sequence; many activities involve multiple intersecting aspects simultaneously
target_learners: learners across diverse educational contexts from elementary school to teacher education
target_learning_goals: fully apt epistemic performance including adaptive, metacognitively regulated, motivated, and socially engaged epistemic thinking
examples: The framework was applied in a case study illustrating how teachers might promote epistemic performance by attending to all five aspects through their activities and discourse
key_sources: Sarit Barzilai & Clark A. Chinn. (2024). The AIR and Apt-AIR Frameworks of Epistemic Performance and Growth: Reflections on Educational Theory Development. Educational Psychology Review. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-024-09927-5

article_title: Advances in Cognitive Psychology Relevant to Education: Introduction to the Special Issue
citation: Pooja K. Agarwal. (2012). Advances in Cognitive Psychology Relevant to Education: Introduction to the Special Issue. Educational Psychol Rev (2012) 24:353–354. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-012-9212-0
title: Apply a century of cognitive psychology research on human learning and memory to real-world education to ground practice in evidence rather than doctrine
description: The article argues that cognitive and educational scientists should, in the author's words, take "what we have learned over the course of at least 100 years about human learning and memory and apply it to the 'real world' of education." By giving research away, scientists could add scientific rigor to education debates, strengthen teacher training standards, and improve data-based decision making, moving practice away from history and doctrine toward evidence-based methods.
requirements: Researchers must widely disseminate evidence-based practices rather than keeping findings within the field
constraints: The article notes that year after year new initiatives are implemented yet often fail to obtain significant improvements, so translation alone is not a quick fix
target_learners: K-12 students in national education systems
target_learning_goals: Improved educational outcomes through evidence-based instructional practices
examples: The special issue itself is presented as an initial step: each article reviews recent advances in learning and memory research and addresses potential implementation of cognitive strategies in authentic classroom settings
key_sources: Pooja K. Agarwal. (2012). Advances in Cognitive Psychology Relevant to Education: Introduction to the Special Issue. Educational Psychol Rev (2012) 24:353–354. https://doi.org/10.1007/s10648-012-9212-0

article_title: Reassessing Aptitude: Introduction to a Special Issue in Honor of Richard E. Snow
citation: Patrick C. Kyllonen & Susanne P. Lajoie (2003). Reassessing Aptitude: Introduction to a Special Issue in Honor of Richard E. Snow. Educational Psychologist, 38(2), 79–83. https://doi.org/10.1207/S15326985EP3802_2
title: Aptitude complexes versus trait complexes: interaction-based and commonality-based configurations of learner variables
description: The article contrasts two frameworks for studying configurations of learner variables. Snow's aptitude complexes treat a complex as an interaction between factors whose interaction term may account for variance in treatment outcomes independently of the components. Ackerman's trait complexes instead treat a complex as a collection of intercorrelating variables, an "amalgamation" of variables that go together, derived from factor analyses of ability, interest, and personality data.
requirements: Single-predictor, single-outcome studies are presumed unfruitful for understanding aptitude–instruction relations; variables must be studied as sets
constraints: The article states the two schemes are complementary rather than competing: Snow's complexes may be most useful for predicting treatment outcomes, Ackerman's for studying coherences among personal characteristics
target_learners: learners characterized by multiple ability, interest, and personality variables
target_learning_goals: predicting instructional treatment outcomes from learner characteristic configurations
examples: Ackerman proposes four trait complexes emerging from factor analyses: social, clerical–convention, science–mathematics, and intellectual–cultural, against Snow's five candidate aptitude complexes
key_sources: Patrick C. Kyllonen & Susanne P. Lajoie (2003). Reassessing Aptitude: Introduction to a Special Issue in Honor of Richard E. Snow. Educational Psychologist, 38(2), 79–83. https://doi.org/10.1207/S15326985EP3802_2

article_title: Academic acceleration in gifted youth and fruitless concerns regarding psychological well-being: A 35-year longitudinal study.
citation: Bernstein Brian O., Lubinski David, Benbow Camilla P. (2021). Academic Acceleration in Gifted Youth and Fruitless Concerns Regarding Psychological Well-Being: A 35-Year Longitudinal Study. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000500
title: Appropriate developmental placement as the general continuum underlying acceleration
description: The article frames acceleration not as an isolated intervention but as one location on a broader best-practice continuum. It states, "The more general dimension is the continuum for what all students require, that is, appropriate developmental placement (Lubinski & Benbow, 2000)." Presenting curriculum at the depth and pace at which a student assimilates new knowledge is beneficial; for talented students, above-level assessments indicate when an above-level curriculum is needed. Several acceleration modalities are described as likely functionally equivalent.
requirements: Above-level assessments (for precocity) are useful in determining when an above-level curriculum (for acceleration) is needed
constraints: The modalities of acceleration studied are described as but a few examples of a broader class of educational interventions for intellectually precocious youth
target_learners: intellectually precocious youth
all students, as the continuum is described as what all students require
target_learning_goals: matching educational curriculum to the depth and pace at which students assimilate new knowledge
examples: The article operationalized acceleration via an acceleration composite (AP courses, college courses, grades skipped) and age of high school graduation, both treated as locations on the placement continuum.
key_sources: Bernstein Brian O., Lubinski David, Benbow Camilla P. (2021). Academic Acceleration in Gifted Youth and Fruitless Concerns Regarding Psychological Well-Being: A 35-Year Longitudinal Study. Journal of Educational Psychology. https://doi.org/10.1037/edu0000500

article_title: An experiment in learning an abstract subject.
citation: Thorndike, E. L., & Upton, C. B. (1922). An Experiment in Learning an Abstract Subject. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 13(6). https://doi.org/10.1037/h0072644
title: Apply each item of fact or principle as soon as learned, give many short problems first, and enable learners to ascertain correctness very soon and very often
description: The experiment corroborates pedagogical doctrines about sequencing and feedback in learning organized abstract subjects. There was general agreement among the adult learners "that each item of fact or principle should be applied as soon as learned, that miscellaneous problems requiring the selection of appropriate principles should be given later, and that many short problems with a minimum of computation" should come first. Learners also agreed the problems explained the text as truly as the text explained the problems, and that correctness should be ascertainable very soon after finishing any part of the work.
requirements: A supply of short problems requiring minimal computation, sample problems solved in the text as illustrations of formulas, and a means for learners to check their work along its course.
constraints: The agreement is the subjects' reported opinion after the experiment, not a manipulated comparison; the article reports no test of these arrangements.
target_learners: adult learners of novel abstract material
high school pupils in abstract subjects
target_learning_goals: understanding and applying principles of electricity and magnetism
mastering organized abstract subject matter
examples: Subjects studied Franklin and Esty's text for six hours, then worked problems 4 to 18 with the textbook answers erased, keeping notes of difficulties.
key_sources: Thorndike, E. L., & Upton, C. B. (1922). An Experiment in Learning an Abstract Subject. The Journal of Educational Psychology, 13(6). https://doi.org/10.1037/h0065229

article_title: Who’s learning? Using within-family studies to understand personalized learning
citation: von Stumm, S. & Wertz, J. (2021). Who's learning? Using within-family studies to understand personalized learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00082-4
title: Aptitude–treatment interaction paradigm as framework for matching instruction to learner characteristics
description: The article describes the aptitude–treatment interaction (ATI) paradigm as the concept that some learning environments are more or less effective for particular individuals depending on their learning abilities and needs. As printed: "The concept that some learning environments are more or less effective for particular individuals, depending on their learning abilities and needs, is known as 'aptitude– treatment interaction' or 'ATI paradigm'". The 'treatment' refers to the environment available to the learner, while 'aptitude' refers to individual differences forecasting success under a given treatment.
requirements: Testing aptitude–treatment effects requires assessing how various degrees of (mis)match between instruction and learner characteristics affect learning outcomes
constraints: The article states aptitude–treatment interactions "have not been conclusively demonstrated" and that testing them in classrooms requires extremely large sample sizes because effect sizes are likely to be small
target_learners: children in formal and informal educational settings
target_learning_goals: optimizing fit between instruction and learner characteristics to maximize learning
key_sources: von Stumm, S. & Wertz, J. (2021). Who's learning? Using within-family studies to understand personalized learning. npj Science of Learning. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41539-020-00082-4

article_title: Adaptive Intelligent Support to Improve Peer Tutoring in Algebra
citation: Walker, E., Rummel, N., & Koedinger, K. R. (2014). Adaptive Intelligent Support to Improve Peer Tutoring in Algebra. Int J Artif Intell Educ 24, 33–61. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0001-9
title: APTA: the Adaptive Peer Tutoring Assistant for high school algebra
description: APTA is an adaptive collaborative learning support environment built on the literal equation solving unit of the Cognitive Tutor Algebra. One student, the tutee, solves equations while the peer tutor watches, marks steps right or wrong, and chats; the system adds adaptive help-giving prompts addressed to the tutor. As the article states, "a second student (the peer tutor) marks the problem steps right or wrong and discusses the problems with the tutee in a chat window." Prompts are visible to both students and posed as non-critical questions to protect the tutor's authority.
requirements: Peer tutors and tutees interact through separate interfaces connected by a central control module
Sentence classifiers must be selected before utterances are typed in the chat window
constraints: In the reported version, prompts were always addressed to the peer tutor, not the tutee
The evaluation retained fixed roles rather than the designed reciprocal role swap
target_learners: High school algebra students in grades 7-12
target_learning_goals: Literal equation solving
Peer tutoring help-giving skills
examples: Students received an average of one prompt in the chat window for every three peer tutor actions after piloting tuning

article_title: Reciprocal Tutoring: Design with Cognitive Load Sharing
citation: Chih-Yueh Chou & Tak-Wai Chan. (2015). Reciprocal Tutoring: Design with Cognitive Load Sharing. International Artificial Intelligence in Education Society. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-015-0083-7
title: Fade scaffolding at an appropriate pace so students do not over-depend on it or become frustrated
description: In the CLS approach, when students become proficient in their assigned sub-tasks, tools should be removed or more sub-tasks distributed to maintain appropriate difficulty. The article warns that pacing matters in both directions: fading too slowly might hinder students from learning sub-tasks whereas fading too rapidly might frustrate students. An appropriate fading of scaffolding guides students to learn and prevents them from excessively depending on scaffolding. Scoring mechanisms based on tutees' help requests have been used to prevent over-dependence on tutors and tools.
requirements: Establishing student models of student knowledge and behavior is crucial in appropriately fading scaffolding
constraints: Fading too slowly hinders learning of sub-tasks; fading too rapidly frustrates students
target_learners: Students progressing from scaffolded tuteeing and tutoring toward independent task completion
target_learning_goals: Completing all sub-tasks of a learning task independently after scaffolding is removed
examples: Table 3 presents an example of scaffolding and fading mechanisms across four learning stages for a novice student, from tuteeing with a tuteeing tool and virtual tutor to serving as tutee and tutor by themselves

article_title: Investigating the Impact of a Collaborative Conversational Agent on Dialogue Productivity and Knowledge Acquisition
citation: Adelson de Araujo, Pantelis M. Papadopoulos, Susan McKenney, Ton de Jong. (2025). Investigating the Impact of a Collaborative Conversational Agent on Dialogue Productivity and Knowledge Acquisition. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-025-00469-7
title: Academically Productive Talk framework with the Four Goals of Productive Discussion
description: The Academically Productive Talk (APT) framework, also known as Accountable Talk, "encourages student interaction and reasoning to ultimately foster a deeper understanding of the subject matter through the strategic use of 'talk moves'", i.e., reflective prompts. It describes dialogue productivity through the Four Goals of Productive Discussion: sharing thoughts; orienting and listening to one another; deepening the reasoning; and engaging with each other's reasoning. The article uses these goals both to design Clair's talk moves and to measure guidance effectiveness.
requirements: Guidance must attend to student dialogue and pose talk moves in a timely manner to help students across aspects of dialogue productivity
constraints: APT talk moves are content-independent, though the article's What-if talk move marks a deviation by directly addressing content
target_learners: secondary school students (14-16-year-old) working in dyads
target_learning_goals: productive collaborative dialogue during inquiry learning
knowledge acquisition in science (digestive system)
examples: Clair's interventions were designed and evaluated against the four goals, with pattern-mining measures per goal

Investigating the Impact of a Collaborative Conversational Agent on Dialogue Productivity and Knowledge Acquisition. article_title: Preface to the Special Issue on Creating and Improving Adaptive Learning: Smart Authoring Tools and Processes
citation: Andrew M. Olney, Stephen B. Gilbert, Kelly Rivers. (2021). Preface to the Special Issue on Creating and Improving Adaptive Learning: Smart Authoring Tools and Processes. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education (2022) 32:1–3. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-021-00277-9
title: Apprentice Learner Architecture for domain-general tutor authoring (MacLellan & Koedinger)
description: One of the four accepted special-issue papers. MacLellan and Koedinger "offer a more technical and generalized treatment of the teachable agent approach using their Apprentice Learner Architecture", covering "diverse tutoring domains including fraction arithmetic, learning chinese characters, correct a/an/the usage, block tower stability, rule induction, stoichiometry, and equations". The editorial places it with Matsuda's work as adaptive authoring of adaptive content.
requirements: Learner models that can be trained across domains, generalizing the teachable-agent approach beyond a single domain
constraints: Classified as adaptive authoring of adaptive content in Table 1
target_learners: tutor authors
teachers and trainers who are not programmers
target_learning_goals: domain-general tutor authoring with teachable learner models
examples: Domains covered include fraction arithmetic, chinese characters, a/an/the usage, block tower stability, rule induction, stoichiometry, and equations

article_title: Domain-General Tutor Authoring with Apprentice Learner Models
citation: Christopher J. MacLellan & Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2022). Domain-General Tutor Authoring with Apprentice Learner Models. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00214-2
title: Apprentice Learner Architecture: a modular framework of knowledge, performance, and learning components for interactive learning from tutors
description: The Apprentice Learner Architecture is a modular framework positing the knowledge structures, performance components, and learning mechanisms needed for apprentice learning—computational models that learn interactively from examples and feedback. It posits four knowledge structures (working memory, relational knowledge, overly-general operators, and skills), three performance components (relational inference, how search, and skill execution), and four learning mechanisms (how-, where-, when-, and which-learning). The architecture is designed to interact with tutoring systems, where agents receive steps, attempt them or request demonstrations, and receive feedback. It unifies mechanisms from prior systems such as ACM, CASCADE, STEPS, and SIMSTUDENT.
requirements: Requires interaction with a tutoring system that can provide steps, demonstrations, and correctness feedback
constraints: The architecture remains intentionally abstract on implementation specifics for each component, as different implementations may be preferable in different circumstances
target_learners: tutor authors and non-programmers building intelligent tutoring systems
target_learning_goals: authoring expert models for tutoring systems across domains
examples: The architecture was used to create two models: the Decision Tree model, which non-incrementally learns skills, and the Trestle model, which learns incrementally
key_sources: Christopher J. MacLellan & Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2022). Domain-General Tutor Authoring with Apprentice Learner Models. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00214-2

article_title: Domain-General Tutor Authoring with Apprentice Learner Models
citation: Christopher J. MacLellan & Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2022). Domain-General Tutor Authoring with Apprentice Learner Models. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00214-2
title: Apprentice learner models enable non-programmers to author tutors for complex domains where existing approaches struggle
description: Apprentice learner models provide a means for non-programmers to build expert models by training computational agents through demonstrations and feedback, similar to how human apprentices learn. Domain experts train models by providing examples and feedback, and these models translate instruction into expert models that can power tutoring systems. This approach generalizes from training, unlike Example-Tracing which does not perform any generalization, making it viable for domains where demonstrating all correct solutions is impractical.
requirements: Requires a tutor interface with a relational representation that the agent can perceive
Requires interactive training with demonstrations and feedback
constraints: Particulars of how the interface was authored impact the agent's learning and performance
target_learners: teachers and other non-programmers building educational technologies
target_learning_goals: authoring pedagogically effective tutoring systems
examples: The Decision Tree model was used to author a novel experimental design tutor, and both models were applied across eight tutor domains
key_sources: Christopher J. MacLellan & Kenneth R. Koedinger. (2022). Domain-General Tutor Authoring with Apprentice Learner Models. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-020-00214-2

article_title: Towards an Agile Approach to Adapting Dynamic Collaboration Support to Student Needs
citation: Adamson, D., Dyke, G., Jang, H., & Rosé, C. P. (2014). Towards an Agile Approach to Adapting Dynamic Collaboration Support to Student Needs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0012-6
title: Academically Productive Talk (APT) framework of facilitation moves for eliciting transactive discussion
description: Academically Productive Talk is a classroom discussion facilitation approach comprising core moves (Revoicing, Press for Reasoning, Challenge, Restate, Add More, Agree/Disagree, Explain Other) that teachers and agents employ to encourage discussions in which students make reasoning public and interact with it transactively. The article maps each move onto three transact dimensions (self/other-oriented, representational/transformational, consensus/conflict-oriented) and proposes these moves as content-independent building blocks for dynamic collaborative learning support. The framework posits a logical ordering of move demand, from self-oriented representational moves to other-oriented transformational conflict-oriented ones.
requirements: Students must receive instruction on APT moves prior to online interaction so agent moves can model and facilitate the discussion style
constraints: The preconditions for successful use of specific APT moves and which learners benefit most from which moves remain unexplored in prior classroom literature
target_learners: high school students
undergraduate students
target_learning_goals: articulate and monitor own reasoning
evaluate and challenge peers' reasoning
build deep understanding of causal mechanisms
examples: The article maps eight APT moves onto transact categories in Table 1, with example teacher utterances such as 'Explain your thinking' and 'Do you agree or disagree, and why?'
key_sources: Adamson, D., Dyke, G., Jang, H., & Rosé, C. P. (2014). Towards an Agile Approach to Adapting Dynamic Collaboration Support to Student Needs. International Journal of Artificial Intelligence in Education. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40593-013-0012-6

article_title: Animated pedagogical agents effects on enhancing student motivation and learning in a science inquiry learning environment
citation: Hans van der Meij, Jan van der Meij, Ruth Harmsen. (2015). Animated pedagogical agents effects on enhancing student motivation and learning in a science inquiry learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-015-9378-5
title: Design motivational agents for science as female, young, attractive, and cool to appeal especially to female students
description: The article's literature review concludes that an agent's external properties can be tuned to maximize motivational impact on female students: "the impact of the APA on female students’ motivation can be maximized by presenting the agent as female, young, attractive and cool". The study implemented this by presenting a female peer-like agent (Emma) of similar age to the participants, designed to look cool, in a kinematics inquiry environment. The design rests on Bandura's model-target similarity claim and on reviewed studies showing embodied, female agents raised female students' science motivation.
requirements: The agent should be embodied (image and voice) rather than voice-only, per the reviewed evidence that embodied APAs were more persuasive
Messages should address task relevance and self-efficacy, e.g., via ARCS relevance and confidence strategies
constraints: The article notes equivocal support for a female agent in math-domain studies, where an earlier study favored a male APA for female students
Emma's design was restricted by the available Elckerlyc models
target_learners: third-year secondary school science students (mean age 14.7)
target_learning_goals: science motivation, specifically task relevance and self-efficacy in physics inquiry learning
examples: Emma was created by linking SimQuest with Elckerlyc and Loquendo, shown as face and upper body, with the role of a fellow student and hard-coded reactions identical for all participants
key_sources: Hans van der Meij, Jan van der Meij, Ruth Harmsen. (2015). Animated pedagogical agents effects on enhancing student motivation and learning in a science inquiry learning environment. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-015-9378-5

article_title: Uncovering variations in learning behaviors and cognitive engagement among students with diverse learning goals and outcomes
citation: Slaviša Radović, Niels Seidel. (2025). Uncovering variations in learning behaviors and cognitive engagement among students with diverse learning goals and outcomes. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-025-10528-4
title: Learner Dashboard in an adaptive personalized learning environment with color-coded progress indicators
description: The studied environment's Learner Dashboard is "a centralized hub for all learning resources", organized by course units in rows so students can monitor progress and access materials at a glance. Resources are categorized by material type to support self-regulation, and a color-coded scheme marks goal-aligned activities in green, potential issues in yellow, and performance inconsistencies in orange. The environment hosted digital texts plus quiz, self-assessment, and expert corrected tasks over an 11-week distance course.
requirements: Voluntary participation with consent to use the platform and the study, in compliance with GDPR regulations
constraints: Participation in the learning environment was voluntary; students could rely on offline printed materials, limiting captured digital traces
target_learners: distance higher education university students
target_learning_goals: self-regulated learning toward passing or mastering a course
monitoring progress across course units
examples: Over an 11-week period, students worked individually with printed and digital texts and digital assignment tasks, culminating in a final exam

article_title: Authenticity in a high school data science curriculum
citation: Rotem Israel-Fishelson, David Weintrop. (2026). Authenticity in a high school data science curriculum. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10622-1
title: Curriculum design characteristics fostering perceived authenticity: flexibility, live data, disciplinary practice structure, and culminating project
description: The article identifies four curriculum-level design characteristics that together fostered students' sense of authentic learning: curricular flexibility enabling pursuit of interest-aligned explorations, grounding activities in live real-time datasets, structuring lessons around core data science practices, and embedding authentic assessment in a culminating project. As the article states, "The curriculum's flexibility boosted Personal Authenticity by enabling students to pursue data exploration activities and projects that resonated with their diverse interests." Each characteristic maps to one of the four thick-authenticity dimensions.
requirements: Datasets and themes selected based on student interests identified through participatory design research
Tools supporting the full data science workflow
A rubric aligned with core data science practices for assessment
constraints: Tensions exist among the four dimensions; focusing on one form of authenticity may impact another
target_learners: high school students in computer science classes
target_learning_goals: data science skills and practices
engagement through personally meaningful inquiry
examples: Across three units of six lessons, students moved from exploring interest-themed datasets toward an open-ended final project with increasing autonomy
key_sources: Rotem Israel-Fishelson, David Weintrop. (2026). Authenticity in a high school data science curriculum. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10622-1

article_title: Authenticity in a high school data science curriculum
citation: Rotem Israel-Fishelson, David Weintrop. (2026). Authenticity in a high school data science curriculum. Education Tech Research Dev. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11423-026-10622-1
title: API Can Code: an interest-driven high school data science curriculum using RapidAPI, EduBlocks, and CODAP
description: API Can Code is "an interest-driven DS curriculum that introduces students to the computational foundations of DS through authentic, meaningful data exploration." It comprises three units of six lessons each: data impact and evaluation, programmatic data retrieval and manipulation from public APIs via EduBlocks, and data analysis and visualization with CODAP, culminating in an open-ended final project. Students query RapidAPI repositories, work with datasets on themes like music, sports, and earthquakes, and present findings to peers with structured slides.
requirements: Teacher professional training; the teacher underwent weekly professional training with two researchers
Support materials including exemplar programs, slides, video tutorials, a glossary, exit tickets, and a validated list of free-to-use APIs
constraints: Each curricular lesson lasted 90 minutes in the same classroom; implemented in two computer science classes at one public charter high school
target_learners: 12th-grade high school students, majority Black/African American, mostly with prior computer science coursework
target_learning_goals: computational foundations of data science
data collection, cleaning, analysis, visualization, and communication
examples: Students retrieved top movies in a preferred genre during a specific period, and final projects used APIs such as dog breed, NFL statistics, and Zillow housing data

article_title: Measures Matter: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Educational Apps on Preschool to Grade 3 Children's Literacy and Math Skills
citation: James Kim, Joshua Gilbert, Qun Yu, Charles Gale. (2021). Measures Matter: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Educational Apps on Preschool to Grade 3 Children's Literacy and Math Skills. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/23328584211004183
title: Science-of-learning account of why educational apps can improve early academic skills
description: The article proposes three mechanisms through which educational apps may improve young children's learning: the touchscreen medium itself, the one-to-one or small-group practice context, and gamified learning affordances. It states that "interactive educational applications can support active, engaging, targeted, and varied practice," that touchscreens spare young children fine-motor keyboard demands, and that apps may provide more time on task with supplemental supports similar to tutoring, plus personalization and gamified elements like scaffolding and rewards.
requirements: Apps must foster active, engaged, meaningful learning with high-quality social interactions and clear learning goals, plus deliberate practice with feedback and interleaved varied activities
constraints: The authors caution results may not generalize to apps neither based on principles from the science of learning nor subjected to rigorous experimental evaluations
target_learners: preschool to Grade 3 children (ages 3–9)
target_learning_goals: literacy and mathematics skills
examples: Berkowitz et al.'s Bedtime Learning Together math app fostering parent-child co-engagement around daily math word problems, and Neuman's Learn With Homer with structured lessons and adult fidelity monitoring, cited as high-quality app examples
key_sources: James Kim, Joshua Gilbert, Qun Yu, Charles Gale. (2021). Measures Matter: A Meta-Analysis of the Effects of Educational Apps on Preschool to Grade 3 Children's Literacy and Math Skills. AERA Open. https://doi.org/10.1177/23328584211004183

article_title: The effectiveness of the problem-based learning teaching model for use in introductory Chinese undergraduate medical courses: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
citation: Zhang Yanqi, Zhou Liang, Liu Xiaoyu, Liu Ling, Wu Yazhou, Zhao Zengwei, Yi Dali, Yi Dong. (2015). The Effectiveness of the Problem-Based Learning Teaching Model for Use in Introductory Chinese Undergraduate Medical Courses: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. PLoS ONE. https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0120884
title: Apply PBL preferentially in laboratory course settings where small-group work aligns with hands-on assessment
description: The article's subgroup analysis and discussion support applying the PBL teaching model preferentially in laboratory course settings, where the authors state that "laboratory courses are typically conducted in small groups, which is more suitable for PBL teaching model adoption" and that laboratory exams "focus more on execution and analytical skills." The meta-analytic evidence shows the examination score advantage of PBL over LBL is roughly three times larger in laboratory courses (SMD = 2.01) than in theory courses (SMD = 0.72).
requirements: Laboratory courses conducted in small groups, as the article states these are more suitable for PBL teaching model adoption
constraints: In theory courses with limited teaching conditions, students may be divided into groups but remain in one classroom that can exceed 100 students, limiting PBL suitability
target_learners: Undergraduate medical students in introductory courses (freshman to junior-year)
target_learning_goals: Execution and analytical skills assessed in laboratory course examinations
examples: The meta-analysis found the laboratory course subgroup examination score SMD was 2.01 versus 0.72 for theory courses, a statistically significant difference (P<0.001).
key_sources: Zhang Yanqi, Zhou Liang, Liu Xiaoyu, Liu Ling, Wu Yazhou, Zhao Zengwei, Yi Dali, Yi Dong. (2015). The Effectiveness of the Problem-Based Learning Teaching Model for Use in Introductory Chinese Undergraduate Medical Courses: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis. article_title: Efficacy of an Online Resource for Teaching Interpersonal Problem Solving Skills to Women Graduate Students in Engineering
citation: Jennifer M. Bekki, Bianca L. Bernstein, Natalie Fabert, Natalie Gildar, and Amy Way. (2014). Efficacy of an Online Resource for Teaching Interpersonal Problem Solving Skills to Women Graduate Students in Engineering. Advances in Engineering Education. https://careerwise.asu.edu
title: Assessment of Problem Solving Skills (APSS) scenario-based instrument and scoring rubrics
description: The APSS is an open-ended, scenario-based assessment containing two questions: the first asks respondents to "list the steps taught by the CareerWISE learning environment to tackle interpersonal problems", and the second, a performance assessment, asks participants to describe how they would apply interpersonal problem solving skills to a realistic graduate-student scenario. Two versions (A and B) present different scenarios derived from focus groups with the target population. Responses were scored with rubrics using four-point coding schemes; inter-rater reliability via Krippendorff's alpha was 95% CI [0.48, 0.58] for Question 1 and 95% CI [0.71, 0.81] for Question 2.
requirements: Effective scoring rubrics and trained scorers are required; a significant time commitment would be required to train and engage scorers in the use of the rubrics.
constraints: The assessments do not evaluate whether the skills are transferable, are based on a single scenario on one occasion immediately following the intervention, and do not evaluate whether participants can enact the skills in real-life settings.
target_learners: Female STEM doctoral students
target_learning_goals: Measuring ability to describe and apply interpersonal problem solving skills
examples: Version A's scenario depicts a main character struggling to get timely feedback from her advisor; Version B's scenario involves a signature needed from an absent advisor to schedule a dissertation defense.
