article_title: The Effect of Keyword Method on Vocabulary Retention of Senior High School EFL Learners in Iran
citation: Davoudi, M., & Yousefi, D. (2016). The Effect of Keyword Method on Vocabulary Retension of Senior High School EFL Learners in Iran. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(11). https://www.iiste.org
title: Educators should apply mnemonic vocabulary training techniques, especially the keyword method, to support L2 word retention
description: The article recommends that vocabulary instruction incorporate mnemonic techniques, particularly the keyword method, because its quasi-experimental results showed significant retention advantages over traditional instruction. It states it is "beneficial for educators to apply vocabulary training techniques s uch as mnemonic techniques specially keyword method". Teachers should also stimulate student motivation for the method and varied vocabulary learning strategies.
requirements: Teachers need to prepare keywords that correlate with the words in the textbook and give learners strategy study sheets to create their own corresponding keywords
constraints: Evidence comes from a single quasi-experimental study with 38 female grade-four students in two intact classes at Iranian public high schools
target_learners: senior high school EFL learners
target_learning_goals: L2 vocabulary acquisition and long-term retention
examples: In the study, the experimental group received a full explanation of the keyword technique and completed keyword strategy study sheets, with seven to eight words taught per session over eight weekly 25-minute sessions.
key_sources: Davoudi, M., & Yousefi, D. (2016). The Effect of Keyword Method on Vocabulary Retension of Senior High School EFL Learners in Iran. Journal of Education and Practice, 7(11). https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1099563

article_title: Validity of a Checklist for the Design, Content, and Instructional Qualities of Children's Books
citation: Erkan Çer, Ertuğrul Şahin. (2016). Validity of a Checklist for the Design, Content, and Instructional Qualities of Children's Books. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.24. https://www.iiste.org
title: Appropriateness for children (child's reality) principle for children's books
description: An organizing principle for evaluating and producing children's books. The article defines it: "The principle of the appropriateness for children m eans taking into account the attention, needs, and language universe of children and being able to match them t o the books they read." It holds that design, content, and instructional qualities should match children's developmental stages and literary criteria, that children must be subjects in the books, and that books must prioritize the child's reality rather than adult values. The checklist validated in this study is grounded in this principle as developed by Çer and Şahin (2016).
requirements: Books must reflect children's developmental stages, language universe, needs, and interests
constraints: The article notes the concept of a child is understood differently in various communities and cultures, which challenges assessment
target_learners: children reading books at primary and secondary school levels
target_learning_goals: developing literary awareness
critical and creative thinking
coping with life difficulties
examples: The study's experimental group received books selected as appropriate for children at primary and secondary school levels based on this principle's criteria
key_sources: Erkan Çer, Ertuğrul Şahin. (2016). Validity of a Checklist for the Design, Content, and Instructional Qualities of Children's Books. Journal of Education and Practice, Vol.7, No.24. https://eric.ed.gov/?id=EJ1112922

article_title: An Intervention Programme for Promoting More Effective Learning among Foundation Phase Learners in South Africa
citation: Ona Janse van Rensburg. (2015). An intervention Programme for Promoting More Effective Learning among Foundation Phase Learners in South Africa. Journal of Curriculum and Teaching, Vol. 4, No. 2. https://doi.org/10.5430/jct.v4n2p110
title: Aptitude Test for School Beginners (HSRC standardized school-readiness test)
description: The measuring instrument used in the experiment is "the Aptitude Test for School Beginners, a standardized culture-free school readiness test of the former Human Sciences Research Council, consisting of a battery of 8 sub-sections (Perception, Spatial, Reasoning, Numerical, Gestalt, Coordination, Memory and Verbal Expression)". It was administered as a pre-test to place participants and repeated as the post-test after the ten weeks; both tests were marked according to prescribed procedures and processed by a university statistics department, with Cohen's (1988) effect sizes used to determine practical significance.
requirements: Marking in accordance with prescribed procedures and interpretation according to the prescribed norms
constraints: Used here with Grade 1 learners aged 6-7 in a South African English-medium school
target_learners: Grade 1 learners aged 6-7
target_learning_goals: Measuring school readiness across perception, spatial, reasoning, numerical, gestalt, coordination, memory and verbal expression sub-sections
examples: Both groups departed from a baseline of 28.5 on the Aptitude Test scale, and the same test was repeated after the ten-week experiment
key_sources: Ona Janse van Rensburg. (2015). An intervention Programme for Promoting More Effective Learning among Foundation Phase Learners in South Africa. Journal of Curriculum and Teaching, Vol. 4, No. 2. https://doi.org/10.5430/jct.v4n2p110

article_title: The Effect of Geogebra on Students' Conceptual and Procedural Knowledge: The Case of Applications of Derivative
citation: Mehmet Fatih Ocal. (2017). The Effect of Geogebra on Students’ Conceptual and Procedural Knowledge: The Case of Applications of Derivative. Higher Education Studies, 7(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/hes.v7n2p67
title: Applications of Derivative Test (ADT)
description: The Applications of Derivative Test is the study's main data collection tool, involving "six open-ended questions, three of which were focusing primarily on procedural knowledge" and three on conceptual knowledge. Each question was graded 0 to 5, yielding total scores of 15 for conceptual and 15 for procedural questions, with a maximum of 30 overall. The test was reviewed by two experienced calculus lecturers and scored with interrater reliability of 92% and 87% for pre- and post-tests.
requirements: Administered as both pre-test and post-test in 50-minute sessions
Rubric with grading criteria prepared and validated by expert lecturers
constraints: Question categorization as conceptual or procedural acknowledges no precise boundary between the two knowledge types (per Star, 2005)
target_learners: undergraduate second-grade pre-service mathematics education students
target_learning_goals: applications of derivative: max-min problems, tangent lines, related rates, interpretation of graphs of functions and derivatives
examples: A procedural question asked for dimensions of the rectangle with largest area bounded by the y-axis, line y=6 and curve y=x2
A conceptual sub-question asked for ranges where f(x) is concave up given the graph of its derivative
key_sources: Mehmet Fatih Ocal. (2017). The Effect of Geogebra on Students’ Conceptual and Procedural Knowledge: The Case of Applications of Derivative. Higher Education Studies, 7(2). https://doi.org/10.5539/hes.v7n2p67

article_title: The Australia New Zealand Microsurgical Skills Course - are we providing a high quality educational programme?
citation: Solanki Jahnvee, Kerdraon Yves, Petsoglou Constantinos, Cornish Elisa, Wilson Graham. (2025). The Australia New Zealand Microsurgical Skills Course - are we providing a high quality educational programme?. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07928-8
title: Apprenticeship model of ophthalmic microsurgical training and its limitations
description: The article describes ophthalmic microsurgical training as "historically based on an apprenticeship model" in which trainees receive one-to-one training from a microsurgical expert. It identifies downfalls including "the cost of prolonged operating time, risk of harm to patients, and inability for trainees to openly ask questions or gain real time feedback due to patient awareness". The article frames wet laboratory and simulation training as a response to these pitfalls, allowing students to practise without time or resource constraints and reducing the risk of post-course intraoperative complications.
constraints: Cost of prolonged operating time
Risk of harm to patients
Inability for trainees to openly ask questions or gain real-time feedback due to patient awareness
target_learners: Ophthalmology trainees
Junior pre-vocational doctors
target_learning_goals: Ophthalmic microsurgical skills
key_sources: Solanki Jahnvee, Kerdraon Yves, Petsoglou Constantinos, Cornish Elisa, Wilson Graham. (2025). The Australia New Zealand Microsurgical Skills Course - are we providing a high quality educational programme?. BMC Medical Education. https://doi.org/10.1186/s12909-025-07928-8

article_title: LapAppendectomy4all: validation of a new methodology for laparoscopic appendectomy simulation and training.
citation: Gonçalves Mário Rui, Marinho Ricardo, Reis Sofia Gaspar, Viveiros Ricardo, Teixeira Manuel Moutinho, Andrade Ana Kam, do Carmo Girão Maria, Rodrigues Pedro Pina-Vaz, Castelo-Branco Sousa Miguel. (2025). LapAppendectomy4all: validation of a new methodology for laparoscopic appendectomy simulation and training. Updates in Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13304-025-02127-y
title: Model-specific objective assessment scale with execution and quality points and graded error categories
description: A purpose-built scoring scale paired with the silicone model. "Trainees start with 0 'Execution points' and 10 'Quality points' and points are summed or rested depending on the performance." Execution points track completion of procedural steps; quality points penalize errors graded as "low quality" > "minor error" > "major error" > "critical error", with fixed deductions (e.g. −0,3 for an unskeletonized appendix, −1,5 for a critical error such as cecal lesion). The authors state no other laparoscopic appendectomy simulator has a specific objective assessment scale adapted to it.
requirements: Photographing the models after simulation so the performed steps and errors can be scored against the scale
constraints: The scale is specific to this model; the authors state other validated scales are "non-model specific or lack some objectivity"
target_learners: first-year general surgery residents
target_learning_goals: objective assessment of laparoscopic appendectomy performance and error awareness
examples: Error deductions illustrated in the article: appendix not skeletonized (−0,3), lost clip (−0,8), finishing without clipping appendix or artery (−1,2), cecum damage (−1,5)
key_sources: Gonçalves Mário Rui, Marinho Ricardo, Reis Sofia Gaspar, Viveiros Ricardo, Teixeira Manuel Moutinho, Andrade Ana Kam, do Carmo Girão Maria, Rodrigues Pedro Pina-Vaz, Castelo-Branco Sousa Miguel. (2025). LapAppendectomy4all: validation of a new methodology for laparoscopic appendectomy simulation and training. Updates in Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s13304-025-02127-y

article_title: Automated performance metrics and surgical gestures: two methods for assessment of technical skills in robotic surgery.
citation: Olsen RG, Svendsen MBS, Tolsgaard MG, Konge L, Røder A, Bjerrum F. (2024). Automated performance metrics and surgical gestures: two methods for assessment of technical skills in robotic surgery. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-024-02051-0
title: A comparative framework of automated performance metrics versus surgical gestures across progression measurement, feedback interpretability, clinical feasibility, and future perspectives
description: The article organizes its comparison of the two assessment methods along four dimensions: ability to measure progression of surgical skills, suitability for understandable feedback, feasibility of acquiring during clinical procedures, and future perspectives. It states APM are "easy to capture in the simulated setting and often good at measuring skills progression but can be difficult to convert to meaningful feedback", while gesture analysis breaks surgery into phases of actions and "can be used to analyze performance patterns throughout a procedure instead of a cumulative score as with the APM". Both methods currently have low clinical feasibility.
requirements: Automatic detection methods for APM and surgical gestures in the clinical setting have not yet been developed
constraints: Manual annotation of surgical procedures is very time-consuming and not scalable
APM are difficult to capture by video analysis and data capture on robot systems is not standard
target_learners: novice robotic surgeons
experienced RARP surgeons
target_learning_goals: assessment of technical surgical skills
feedback on surgical performance
examples: Table 1 compares the two methods across the four dimensions; the study operationalized both methods as composite z-scores with contrasting-groups pass/fail levels.
key_sources: Olsen RG, Svendsen MBS, Tolsgaard MG, Konge L, Røder A, Bjerrum F. (2024). Automated performance metrics and surgical gestures: two methods for assessment of technical skills in robotic surgery. Journal of Robotic Surgery. https://doi.org/10.1007/s11701-024-02051-0

article_title: Assessing trainee critical thinking skills using a novel interactive online learning tool.
citation: Jantausch Barbara A., Bost James E., Bhansali Priti, Hefter Yosefa, Greenberg Isabella, Goldman Ellen. (2023). Assessing trainee critical thinking skills using a novel interactive online learning tool. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2023.2178871
title: American Philosophical Association (APA) critical thinking framework adapted for interactive online assessment of medical trainees
description: The APA framework holds that critical thinking is 'purposeful, reflective judgment based on the consideration of evidence, methods and standards in decision making', with six core skills as its foundation: interpretation, analysis, evaluation, inference, explanation, and self-regulation. This article adapts the framework for the first time, per the authors, into interactive online learning and assessment in medical trainees, operationalizing interpretation, analysis and explanation as open-ended case-based test questions modeled on the California Critical Thinking Skills Test questioning technique, with answers graded against the compiled responses of five malaria experts.
requirements: Test questions must be tailored to the core critical thinking skills the educators wish to study, using the CCTST questioning technique with generic prompters
constraints: This study focused on interpretation, analysis, and explanation, as particularly important in the practice of infectious diseases, rather than all six skills
target_learners: undergraduate and graduate medical trainees
target_learning_goals: critical thinking in clinical diagnosis and management
examples: Pre- and post-test items asked, for example, for a differential diagnosis with reasoning (interpretation), the relationship between an anti-malarial drug and EKG changes (analysis), and justification of a treatment choice (explanation)
key_sources: Jantausch Barbara A., Bost James E., Bhansali Priti, Hefter Yosefa, Greenberg Isabella, Goldman Ellen. (2023). Assessing trainee critical thinking skills using a novel interactive online learning tool. Medical Education Online. https://doi.org/10.1080/10872981.2023.2178871
